clips.text: der Brief
der Brief. Ich schreibe einen Brief.
Ich schreibe einen Brief.
Learn der Brief → die Briefe. In Ich schreibe einen Brief, einen means a: Brief receives the action, so masculine ein changes to einen. Brief keeps its capital B. Its long ee sound is written ie.
Der Brief ist für dich.
die Briefe
One letter: der Brief. Several letters: die Briefe. Add -e. Use die for the plural in this naming exercise; articles can change in other sentence roles.
der
Brief is masculine: der Brief.
A brief message can go in a letter. English brief and German Brief share the same letters, but der Brief means the letter itself.
Learn der Brief together. Capital B; ie, not ei. More than one: die Briefe.
Picture a letter wearing a big capital B. On its envelope is a tiny label: der. Open the envelope and find the letters i then e inside.
ie, not ei. Capital B. Say the article with it: der Brief.
sich fühlen
sich fühlen. Ich fühle mich gut.
Ich fühle mich gut.

English says I feel good. German says Ich fühle mich gut: it needs mich here, although English does not say myself. Match ich → mich, du → dich, wir → uns. For ü, try saying ee with rounded lips, then listen and copy the German sound. Keep the h after ü.
Wir fühlen uns müde.
mich
With ich, use mich: Ich fühle mich gut.
dich
With du, use dich: Du fühlst dich müde.
Before a match: Ich fühle mich gut — I feel good. German needs mich here, even though English does not say myself. Learn the whole phrase together.
sich fühlen: ü, then h. Keep sich when learning the verb; use mich with ich.
Picture a feelings thermometer. The two dots over ü are its two eyes, checking how you feel. Point at yourself when you say mich.
ü has two dots; a silent h follows it. Keep sich with the infinitive.
Before a match, check how you feel: Ich fühle mich gut — I feel good. The feeling is about you, so keep the ‘myself’ part: mich.
sich ärgern
sich ärgern. Ich ärgere mich über den Lärm.
Ich ärgere mich über den Lärm.

Learn sich ärgern über …: to get annoyed about something. Ich ärgere mich means I get annoyed; wir ärgern uns means we get annoyed. English leaves out myself/ourselves here, but German needs mich/uns. Start ärgern with ä.
Wir ärgern uns über den Regen.
Ich pairs with mich. The extra e in ärgere belongs to the ich form.
uns
Wir pairs with uns: Wir ärgern uns.
Someone's loud video interrupts your homework. Ich ärgere mich über den Lärm. Ärger means annoyance or trouble; here you are getting annoyed by the noise.
Write sich ärgern: initial ä, then rgern. Ich uses ärgere mich; wir uses ärgern uns.
Imagine the two dots over ä turning into annoyed eyebrows. A noisy alarm makes you point at yourself: Ich ärgere mich!
Start with ä, then r-g-ern. In ich ärgere, the ending changes to -e.
traurig
traurig. Ich bin traurig.
Ich bin traurig.
Ich bin traurig means I am sad. Spell trau + rig. The au sounds like ow in cow. Listen to the German ending: even when it sounds like ich, write ig. Traurig is sad; müde is tired.
Mein Freund ist traurig.
Your friend moves away: traurig means sad. It’s a feeling, not tiredness. Learn the word in two short spelling blocks: trau + rig.
Keep au together. End with rig: the final written letter is g, even if it sounds different.
Picture a sad face on a rainy window. Draw a tiny tear next to traurig. Pair it with the opposite: glücklich, happy.
Two chunks: trau + rig. Keep au together and end with g, not ch.
der Job
der Job. Mein Vater hat einen Job.
Mein Vater hat einen Job.
Learn der Job → die Jobs: the plural adds s. German nouns need a capital. In Mein Vater hat einen Job, einen means a; masculine ein changes to einen for the thing someone has.
Der Job ist interessant.
die Jobs
Add -s: Job → Jobs.
Job is masculine: der Job.
Easy transfer: a job is der Job. You already know the English spelling; the new information is the German article and capital letter.
der Job: capital J. Plural die Jobs adds s, just like English.
Imagine a job badge with a giant J. The badge belongs to DER boss. The word already looks familiar from English.
Capital J, article der. Add s for the plural: Jobs.
mitkommen
mitkommen. Ich komme mit.
Ich komme mit.

mitkommen means come along. Learn Ich komme mit — I am coming along. Change the verb for the person: du kommst, wir kommen. In these simple statements, keep mit at the end. The dictionary form mitkommen is one word, with double m.
Ich komme heute mit.
Du kommst heute mit.
komme mit
Conjugate kommen → komme. Put mit at the end: Ich komme heute mit.
kommen mit
With wir, use kommen. The prefix mit goes at the end.
Friends head to the park and invite you along. Mit means with; kommen means come. Ich komme mit. Picture joining their group at the door.
Write mitkommen as one infinitive, with double m in kommen. In Ich komme mit, mit moves to the end.
Your friend says “Come along!” Two m letters walk side by side. In a sentence, mit runs ahead to wait at the very end.
Two m letters in kommen. Join mitkommen in the infinitive; split komme … mit in a statement.
umziehen
umziehen. Wir ziehen nach Berlin um.
Wir ziehen nach Berlin um.

Here umziehen means move home, not walk across a room. Ich ziehe um — I am moving. Wir ziehen um — We are moving. In these statements um goes last. In ziehen, ie makes a long ee sound and is followed by a silent h.
Ich ziehe morgen um.
ziehen um
Wir ziehen morgen um. The prefix um goes at the end.
ziehe um
Ich needs ziehe. Keep um at the end.
Think moving house, not walking across the room: Wir ziehen um — We’re moving. Keep the moving verb as one word when naming it: umziehen.
um + ziehen. In ziehen, write ie followed by h. In Wir ziehen um, um goes last.
Imagine a moving box marked um. Inside, i and e stand in order next to a tall h. The box moves to the end: Wir ziehen um.
ie, then h. Infinitive umziehen is one word.
weit weg
weit weg. Meine Freundin wohnt weit weg.
Meine Freundin wohnt weit weg.
weit means far; weg means away. Keep two words: weit weg. In weit, ei sounds like English eye. Hear the final sound in weg, but remember the written ending is g.
Berlin ist weit weg.
Your base is far away on the map: weit weg. Two separate words, two w starts. The space is part of the answer.
weit has ei; weg ends in g. Keep a space between them.
Imagine two signposts far apart: WEIT on one, WEG on the other. The big gap reminds you to put a space between the words.
Two words, both starting with w. First word has ei; second ends in g.
fast
fast. Ich bin fast fertig.
Ich bin fast fertig.
False friend! German fast means almost. English fast would usually be schnell.
Es ist fast acht Uhr.
Your download is at 99%: fast fertig — almost finished. German fast means almost, not speedy. Think nearly done, not going quickly.
Same letters as English fast; different meaning. Write f-a-s-t, with no extra letters.
Imagine a race runner ALMOST at the finish. Freeze the picture just before the line. German fast means almost, even though English fast makes you think of speed.
f-a-s-t. The spelling is familiar; the meaning is the trap.
sich treffen
sich treffen. Wir treffen uns im Park.
Wir treffen uns im Park.
Double f: treffen. For meeting each other, use uns with wir and euch with ihr.
Ich treffe mich mit Ben.
Wir treffen uns means we meet each other.
euch
With ihr, use euch: Ihr trefft euch.
Meet your friend at spawn: Wir treffen uns — We meet up. The two f letters make a simple pair to remember: two friends meeting.
sich treffen: double f, one t at the start. Learn sich too; wir takes uns.
Picture the two f letters as two friends meeting in a park. They stand together in the middle of treffen.
Double f. Include sich in the vocabulary form; wir treffen uns in a sentence.
beide
beide. Wir sind beide müde.
Wir sind beide müde.
beide means both of two: Wir sind beide müde — We are both tired. In beide, ei sounds like English eye. Contrast einige: some or several, without specifying exactly two.
Die zwei Freunde kommen beide.
Two players, and both are ready: beide. Both means exactly two; don’t mix it up with einige, which means some or several.
b + ei + de. The vowel pair is ei, not ie; finish with e.
Hold up exactly two fingers. Both fingers stand over ei in beide. Both means two, not just some.
ei, not ie. End with de.
der Fahrradtrial
der Fahrradtrial. Der Fahrradtrial ist schwer.
Der Fahrradtrial ist schwer.

Bike trials involves balancing and riding over obstacles, not following a trail. Build Fahr + rad + trial; the r letters meet. Your class sheet uses der Fahrradtrial → die Fahrradtrials. The sporting word Trial is normally das Trial; ask your teacher about this article difference. These exercises follow the sheet.
Ich finde den Fahrradtrial spannend.
die Fahrradtrials
In this lesson, use der Fahrradtrial and die Fahrradtrials.
Learn the article supplied in your lesson: der Fahrradtrial.
Bike trials means balancing a bike over obstacles, not riding a trail. Build the name from Fahr + rad + trial; the r letters meet at the join.
Your class sheet uses der Fahrradtrial. Keep capital F, the rr join, and trial with i before a.
Imagine a bike balancing over three blocks labeled Fahr, rad, trial. The r at the end of Fahr bumps into the r at the start of rad: rr.
Capital F, two r letters at the join. Learn der Fahrradtrial. Finish trial, not trail.
hochfahren
hochfahren. Ich fahre den Berg hoch.
Ich fahre den Berg hoch.

hochfahren means ride or drive up. Compare Ich fahre hoch — I ride up; Er fährt hoch — He rides up. With er, a changes to ä; wir keeps fahren. In these simple statements hoch goes at the end. Keep the silent h in fahren.
Wir fahren den Berg hoch.
fahre hoch
Ich fahre den Berg hoch. The prefix hoch goes at the end.
fährt hoch
Compare ich fahre and er fährt: with er, a changes to ä and the ending is t. Er fährt den Berg hoch — He rides up the mountain. Put hoch at the end.
Ride up a hill: hoch means up, fahren means travel by vehicle. Together: hochfahren. In Ich fahre hoch, the up part moves to the end.
hoch + fahren. Keep ch in hoch and the h after a in fahren.
Imagine a bike going hoch (up) a hill. At the summit, hoch is waiting at the end of the sentence: Ich fahre den Berg hoch.
hoch ends in ch; fahren contains h after a. Er fährt adds ä.
hoffentlich
hoffentlich. Hoffentlich kommt sie mit.
Hoffentlich kommt sie mit.
Split it: hoffen + tlich. There are two f letters and a t before lich.
Sie kommt hoffentlich mit.
Wir treffen uns hoffentlich morgen.
Before opening a chest: Hoffentlich! — Hopefully! Link it to hoffen, meaning to hope. For spelling, build hoffen + t + lich; don’t lose that linking t.
Double f, then the t before lich. End with ch, not ck.
Imagine two fingers crossed for hope: ff. Beside them stands a tiny T-shaped sign pointing to lich. Hopefully your wish comes true.
Double f AND the t: hoffen + t + lich.
die Treppe
die Treppe. Die Treppe ist hoch.
Die Treppe ist hoch.

die Treppe means one staircase. English often calls this the stairs, but German Treppe is singular. Multiple staircases: die Treppen. Keep capital T and double p. Ich gehe die Treppe hoch means I am going up the stairs.
Ich gehe die Treppe hoch.
die Treppen
One staircase: die Treppe. Several staircases: die Treppen. Add n. English the stairs can describe just one German Treppe.
die
Treppe is feminine: die Treppe.
At school, you take the staircase to the next floor: Ich gehe die Treppe hoch. Picture the actual steps you use each day.
die Treppe is one staircase, often called the stairs in English. Several staircases: die Treppen. Keep capital T, double p, and final e in Treppe.
Imagine the two p letters as two steps in a staircase. A sign at the bottom says die; a capital T stands at the top.
Capital T and double p. Plural adds n: Treppen.
Write die Treppe with capital T, double p, and final e. Plural: die Treppen.
stark
stark. Mein Bruder ist stark.
Mein Bruder ist stark.
Picture someone lifting something heavy: stark = strong. Finish with rk.
Wir sind stark.
Tony Stark has a strong suit. Use Stark as a name hook for stark — strong. The German adjective stays lowercase; this is a memory link, not a translation rule.
st + ark. Finish rk, with no vowel between r and k. Lowercase s.
Picture a strong person lifting the letters r and k like two heavy weights. The word ends with both weights: rk.
st at the start, rk at the end. No extra vowel between r and k.
streiten
streiten. Wir streiten oft.
Wir streiten oft.

streiten means argue: wir streiten — we argue. Use ich streite, but er streitet: the extra e before t helps you say the ending. The ei sounds like English eye. Arguing is an action; sich ärgern means feeling annoyed.
Die Freunde streiten nicht.
streite
For ich, drop -n from streiten: ich streite.
streitet
The er form is streitet. The extra e makes the ending pronounceable.
Two teammates argue about the plan: Sie streiten — They argue. This is the argument itself; sich ärgern is feeling annoyed.
str + ei + ten. Three consonants at the start; ei, not ie.
Imagine two friends arguing over who goes first: e or i. Settle it: e goes before i in streiten.
Start str; use ei, not ie. The ending is -ten.
müde
müde. Ich bin müde.
Ich bin müde.
Ich bin müde — I am tired. For ü, try ee with rounded lips, then listen and copy the German sound. Keep the dots: u is a different vowel. Spell mü + de. Needing sleep is müde, not traurig (sad).
Nach der Schule sind wir müde.
After a late gaming session: Ich bin müde — I’m tired. Keep it separate from traurig: you need sleep, not cheering up.
m + ü + de. The two dots belong to ü; plain u is a different letter.
Picture a tired face. The two dots over ü are sleepy eyes. Put the eyes back before you let the word go to bed.
Four letters: m-ü-d-e. The umlaut is part of the letter.
schlecht
schlecht. Das Wetter ist schlecht.
Das Wetter ist schlecht.
schlecht means bad. Build sch + le + ch + t. The first sch sounds like English sh; the later ch is a different German sound, not English ch in chair. Listen and copy. Keep both h letters.
Der Film ist schlecht.
A bad connection makes the game lag: schlecht means bad. Build its spelling in four blocks: sch / le / ch / t.
Start sch. There is another ch before the final t; don’t drop that second h.
Imagine a BAD weather report. Rain falls on a sign split into four pieces: sch / le / ch / t. Rebuild it before the storm arrives.
There is ch inside sch at the start, and another ch before the last t.
verliebt
verliebt. Ich bin verliebt.
Ich bin verliebt.
Liebe means love. Build ver + lieb + t: verliebt means in love. Ich bin verliebt — I am in love. The ie sounds like ee; keep written bt even when the b sounds like p.
Sie ist verliebt.
Liebe means love; verliebt means in love. The shared lieb gives you the meaning and the tricky ie spelling in one useful link.
ver + lieb + t. Keep ie together; finish bt, not pt.
Picture a love note folded around ie. A little b and t seal the end of the note together.
ie, not ei. Finish with bt, not pt.
bestimmt
bestimmt. Er kommt bestimmt mit.
Er kommt bestimmt mit.
In this lesson, bestimmt means definitely. Double m: be-stimmt.
Das ist bestimmt richtig.
‘Will you join us?’ ‘Definitely!’ That confident answer is bestimmt in this lesson. It’s a yes with confidence, not just a hopeful maybe.
be + stimmt. Double m followed by t; don’t shorten the ending to one m.
Imagine a big DEFINITELY stamp. Two m-shaped stamp handles press down together, with a final t as the stamp’s handle.
Double m, then t. The whole ending is -immt.
glücklich
glücklich. Ich bin glücklich.
Ich bin glücklich.

Ich bin glücklich — I am happy. Build Glück + lich, then use a lowercase g for the adjective. Keep ü, ck, and the different ending ch. Compare glücklich (happy) and traurig (sad). Listen to ü and ch before repeating.
Meine Freunde sind glücklich.
Glück means luck or happiness. Finding diamonds can make you glücklich — happy. The useful spelling link is Glück + lich, with a lowercase start for the adjective.
glücklich: lowercase g, ü, ck, then lich. The ending is ch, not ck.
Glück means luck or happiness. Imagine finding a lucky coin and smiling: glücklich. The two dots over ü are your happy eyes.
ü + ck, then lich. There is no extra k after lich.
sensibel
sensibel. Mein Freund ist sensibel.
Mein Freund ist sensibel.
Another false friend: sensibel means sensitive, not sensible. It ends in -bel.
Sie ist sehr sensibel.
A friend notices when someone's joke hurts another person. Mein Freund ist sensibel. The shared sensi in sensitive and sensibel anchors the meaning: sensitive.
Write sensibel with ending bel, not ble. It means sensitive, not the English sensible.
Picture a sensitive person noticing a tiny sound from a bell. Let that bell remind you of the ending -bel, with only one l.
sen-si-bel, not the English word sensible. Meaning: sensitive.
fleißig
fleißig. Sie ist fleißig.
Sie ist fleißig.
fleißig means hard-working: Sie ist fleißig — She works hard. Build fleiß + ig. The ei sounds like English eye; ß sounds like s, not b. Keep the written ending ig. Use the ß key below the answer box.
Wir sind fleißig.
Your friend keeps working on a build, even when it takes a few tries. Sie ist fleißig — She is hard-working. Think steady effort, not finishing fast.
fleiß + ig: ei sounds like eye; ß sounds like s, not b. Keep the written ending ig and use the ß button.
Imagine a hard-working student carefully writing ei and then a big ß on a checklist. Every detail gets checked.
ei, then ß, then ig. For this German lesson use ß, even though Swiss spelling uses ss.
A classmate steadily researches, writes, and improves a project. Sie ist fleißig. Fleiß means diligence; the adjective describes the person putting in that work.
Write fleißig with ei, ß, and final ig. Keep the lesson's ß spelling.
zuhören
zuhören. Ich höre dir zu.
Ich höre dir zu.

Learn Ich höre dir zu — I am listening to you. German uses dir, not dich, with zuhören: learn höre dir zu as a phrase. Wir hören dir zu — We are listening to you. In these simple statements zu goes last. Listen to ö; it is not the same sound as o.
Wir hören der Lehrerin zu.
höre zu
Ich höre dir zu. Keep ö in höre and put zu at the end.
hören zu
Wir hören dir zu. The prefix zu goes at the end.
A friend explains something important, and you put your phone down. Ich höre dir zu. Hören means hear; the added zu marks listening attentively to someone.
Write zuhören with ö. Learn höre dir zu as a phrase: listening to you. German uses dir here, not dich. In Ich höre dir zu, zu goes last.
Imagine the dots over ö as two ears listening. The word zu walks to the end while those ears listen: Ich höre dir zu.
ö, not o. Join zuhören in the infinitive; split höre … zu in a statement.
Write zuhören with ö. In Ich höre dir zu, zu goes last; dir is the dative form for you.
einige
einige. Einige Freunde kommen mit.
Einige Freunde kommen mit.
einige means some or several. It does not mean exactly two; that is beide.
Wir haben einige Bücher.
Ich schreibe einige Briefe.
You have some blocks left, not necessarily two: einige. Contrast beide, meaning both of two. Spell it in three small blocks: ei + ni + ge.
Start ei, not ie. Keep the middle i: ei-ni-ge ends in e.
Imagine a basket with some apples. Label three parts of the basket ei / ni / ge. There are several apples, not exactly two.
Start ei, not ie. Three chunks: ei-ni-ge.
sich interessieren
sich interessieren. Ich interessiere mich für Musik.
Ich interessiere mich für Musik.

There are two r letters, neither doubled: one in inter and another in ieren. Keep double s: inter + ess + ieren. Learn Ich interessiere mich für Musik — I am interested in music. German needs mich and für here; do not translate English in word for word.
Wir interessieren uns für Sport.
Ich pairs with mich. Für means in in this expression.
Wir pairs with uns: Wir interessieren uns für Sport.
Think of an interest you actually have: games, music, or sports. sich interessieren means to be interested. Use four spelling blocks: inter / ess / ier / en.
Two r letters, neither doubled: one in inter, another in ier. Double s; ie in ier. Learn sich interessieren für: to be interested in.
Imagine an interesting museum. One r guards the entrance in inter; two s letters are the exhibits in ess. Follow the signs: inter / ess / ier / en.
inter has one r. ess has two s letters. Keep ie in -ieren. Include sich.
One r in inter; double s in ess; ie in ier. Include sich when naming the verb.
Learn der Brief as one piece. Nouns start with a capital letter. Plural: die Briefe.
Add -e: Brief → Briefe. All plural nouns use die.
The ü matters. Change sich with the person: ich fühle mich, du fühlst dich, wir fühlen uns.
ärgern starts with ä. Learn the whole phrase: sich ärgern. Ich ärgere mich means I get annoyed.
Picture a sad face. Say trau-rig in two parts. It ends in -ig, not -ich.
Same word as English, but German adds a capital J and der. Plural: die Jobs.
mit + kommen = come along. In a simple statement, mit moves to the end: Ich komme mit.
Here umziehen means move home. Split it: ziehen … um. Keep ie together in ziehen.
Two words: weit means far, weg means away. Remember the space.
beide means exactly two. Keep ei in that order: b-e-i-d-e.
A bike trial is riding over obstacles. Build the spelling: Fahr + rad + trial. The two r letters meet in Fahrrad. Plural: die Fahrradtrials.
hoch means up; fahren means go by vehicle or ride. In a statement, split fahren … hoch.
Er uses fährt, with ä. The prefix hoch goes at the end.
Learn die Treppe. Double p, and a capital T. Plural: die Treppen.
Add -n: Treppe → Treppen.
Keep ei in streiten. The lesson uses streiten; wir streiten means we argue.
The two dots matter: müde, not mude. Think of feeling tired after a long school day.
Build it: sch + lecht. Watch the ch before the final t.
ver + liebt. Keep ie, then bt. With sein: Ich bin verliebt.
Build Glück + lich. Keep ü and ck. glücklich is happy; traurig is sad.
Keep ei and ß: fl-ei-ß-ig. Use the ß key below the answer box.
zu + hören. The ö matters. In a statement: Ich höre dir zu. Listening to someone uses dative, here dir.
One r, double s: inter-ess-ieren. Use sich interessieren für, with mich for ich.
das Oktoberfest
das Oktoberfest. Das Oktoberfest ist ein Fest.
Das Oktoberfest ist ein Fest.

das Oktoberfest means Oktoberfest festival. die Oktoberfeste means Oktoberfest celebrations. For several separate celebrations, add -e. The famous Munich event is normally named in the singular. Write Oktober with k, not the English c. Join Oktober and fest into one word; capital O. Learn the whole noun with its article. All German nouns start with a capital letter.
Das Oktoberfest ist in München.
die Oktoberfeste
Singular: das Oktoberfest. Plural: die Oktoberfeste. For several separate celebrations, add -e. The famous Munich event is normally named in the singular.
das
For one, say das Oktoberfest; for more than one, say die Oktoberfeste.
Picture an October festival with music and a giant pretzel. Oktober + Fest joins October and festival.
Write Oktober with k, not the English c. Join Oktober and fest into one word; capital O.
Picture the scene, cover the German, and write das Oktoberfest. Check every letter and the article.
das Erntedankfest
das Erntedankfest. Das Erntedankfest ist im Herbst.
Das Erntedankfest ist im Herbst.

das Erntedankfest means harvest thanksgiving festival. die Erntedankfeste means harvest thanksgiving festivals. Add -e for several festivals. Build Ernte + dank + fest without spaces. Keep the e in Ernte and the k in dank. Learn the whole noun with its article. All German nouns start with a capital letter.
Wir feiern das Erntedankfest.
die Erntedankfeste
Singular: das Erntedankfest. Plural: die Erntedankfeste. Add -e for several festivals.
For one, say das Erntedankfest; for more than one, say die Erntedankfeste.
Picture a harvest table: crops, a thank-you sign, and a festival. Ernte is harvest, Dank is thanks, and Fest is festival. It is not the American Thanksgiving holiday.
Build Ernte + dank + fest without spaces. Keep the e in Ernte and the k in dank.
Picture the scene, cover the German, and write das Erntedankfest. Check every letter and the article.
die Wanderung
die Wanderung. Die Wanderung ist lang.
Die Wanderung ist lang.

die Wanderung means hike. die Wanderungen means hikes. Add -en: Wanderung → Wanderungen. Write Wander + ung: only one r in Wander. The noun ending -ung is a useful clue for die. Learn the whole noun with its article. All German nouns start with a capital letter.
Wir machen eine Wanderung.
die Wanderungen
Singular: die Wanderung. Plural: die Wanderungen. Add -en: Wanderung → Wanderungen.
For one, say die Wanderung; for more than one, say die Wanderungen.
Picture a long hike along a forest trail. Connect Wanderung with English wander, but remember: this word names the hike.
Write Wander + ung: only one r in Wander. The noun ending -ung is a useful clue for die.
Picture the scene, cover the German, and write die Wanderung. Check every letter and the article.
der Baum
der Baum. Der Baum ist groß.
Der Baum ist groß.

der Baum means tree. die Bäume means trees. Change a → ä and add -e. Singular Baum has au. Plural Bäume changes a to ä and adds e. Do not put the umlaut in the singular. Learn the whole noun with its article. All German nouns start with a capital letter.
Der Baum hat Blätter.
die Bäume
Singular: der Baum. Plural: die Bäume. Change a → ä and add -e.
For one, say der Baum; for more than one, say die Bäume.
Picture one blocky tree; now add another tree and two dots over the a. One Baum becomes several Bäume.
Singular Baum has au. Plural Bäume changes a to ä and adds e. Do not put the umlaut in the singular.
Picture the scene, cover the German, and write der Baum. Check every letter and the article.
das Blatt
das Blatt. Das Blatt ist gelb.
Das Blatt ist gelb.

das Blatt means leaf. die Blätter means leaves. Change a → ä and add -er. Blatt ends in double t. Blätter keeps tt, changes a to ä, and adds er. Learn the whole noun with its article. All German nouns start with a capital letter.
Das Blatt fällt.
die Blätter
Singular: das Blatt. Plural: die Blätter. Change a → ä and add -er.
For one, say das Blatt; for more than one, say die Blätter.
Picture a leaf falling beside a tree. Give its stem two little branches to remind you of the two t letters. The word can also mean a sheet of paper; this wave uses leaf.
Blatt ends in double t. Blätter keeps tt, changes a to ä, and adds er.
Picture the scene, cover the German, and write das Blatt. Check every letter and the article.
das Bauernhaus
das Bauernhaus. Das Bauernhaus ist alt.
Das Bauernhaus ist alt.

das Bauernhaus means farmhouse. die Bauernhäuser means farmhouses. Only the house part changes: Haus → Häuser; keep Bauern unchanged. Keep the n in Bauern. Singular ends haus; plural ends häuser, with ä. Capital B, no space. Learn the whole noun with its article. All German nouns start with a capital letter.
Das Bauernhaus ist auf dem Bauernhof.
die Bauernhäuser
Singular: das Bauernhaus. Plural: die Bauernhäuser. Only the house part changes: Haus → Häuser; keep Bauern unchanged.
For one, say das Bauernhaus; for more than one, say die Bauernhäuser.
Picture the farmer’s house beside a field. Bauern + Haus builds one farmhouse word. Haus looks a little like English house.
Keep the n in Bauern. Singular ends haus; plural ends häuser, with ä. Capital B, no space.

der Kürbis
der Kürbis. Der Kürbis ist orange.
Der Kürbis ist orange.

der Kürbis means pumpkin. die Kürbisse means pumpkins. Add -se to Kürbis: the resulting ending is -isse, with ss. Kürbis has ü, one s, and no final e. Kürbisse has double s and a final e. Learn the whole noun with its article. All German nouns start with a capital letter.
Der Kürbis ist groß.
die Kürbisse
Singular: der Kürbis. Plural: die Kürbisse. Add -se to Kürbis: the resulting ending is -isse, with ss.
For one, say der Kürbis; for more than one, say die Kürbisse.
Picture a pumpkin with two seeds above it: the two dots belong over ü. On the pumpkin’s label, check Kürbis before adding more pumpkins.
Kürbis has ü, one s, and no final e. Kürbisse has double s and a final e.
Picture the scene, cover the German, and write der Kürbis. Check every letter and the article.
der Igel
der Igel. Der Igel ist klein.
Der Igel ist klein.

der Igel means hedgehog. die Igel means hedgehogs. The noun spelling does not change; change the article der → die. Start with capital I, then gel. The long first vowel is written with just I: do not add an e. Learn the whole noun with its article. All German nouns start with a capital letter.
Der Igel hat Stacheln.
die Igel
Singular: der Igel. Plural: die Igel. The noun spelling does not change; change the article der → die.
For one, say der Igel; for more than one, say die Igel.
Picture one hedgehog, then a family of hedgehogs. Their name stays Igel; only der changes to die.
Start with capital I, then gel. The long first vowel is written with just I: do not add an e.

die Laterne
die Laterne. Die Laterne leuchtet.
Die Laterne leuchtet.

die Laterne means lantern. die Laternen means lanterns. Add -n to Laterne. Say and write La-ter-ne. Keep the e between t and r, and the final e. Laternen adds n. Learn the whole noun with its article. All German nouns start with a capital letter.
Die Laterne ist bunt.
die Laternen
Singular: die Laterne. Plural: die Laternen. Add -n to Laterne.
For one, say die Laterne; for more than one, say die Laternen.
Picture carrying a bright lantern on an autumn evening. English lantern and German Laterne share many letters; look carefully at the different ending.
Say and write La-ter-ne. Keep the e between t and r, and the final e. Laternen adds n.
Picture the scene, cover the German, and write die Laterne. Check every letter and the article.
neblig
neblig. Es ist neblig.
Es ist neblig.

For this lesson, learn neblig: neb-lig. Nebelig is also a correct German spelling, but your assigned word is neblig. The last three letters are lig. Keep lowercase n. In these sentences the describing word comes after ist or sind; use neblig unchanged. The other sentence words are supplied: you only fill in the describing word.
Der Morgen ist neblig.
Picture fog hiding the trees. Nebel means fog; neblig describes foggy weather. Compare Nebel with neblig: the middle e disappears.

trüb
trüb. Der Tag ist trüb.
Der Tag ist trüb.

Only four letters: t-r-ü-b. Keep ü; no final e. Listen to the rounded ü sound. In these sentences the describing word comes after ist or sind; use trüb unchanged. The other sentence words are supplied: you only fill in the describing word.
Das Wetter ist trüb.
Picture a gray, gloomy sky with no bright sunshine. Two little clouds above the word remind you of the two dots on ü. Trüb describes dull weather here, not a sad person.
Only four letters: t-r-ü-b. Keep ü; no final e. Listen to the rounded ü sound.

malerisch
malerisch. Das Dorf ist malerisch.
Das Dorf ist malerisch.

Build maler + isch. The last four letters are isch; keep the three-letter sch together. In these sentences the describing word comes after ist or sind; use malerisch unchanged. The other sentence words are supplied: you only fill in the describing word.
Die Landschaft ist malerisch.
Picture a village so beautiful that a painter wants to paint it. Maler means painter; malerisch means picturesque, like a lovely picture.
Build maler + isch. The last four letters are isch; keep the three-letter sch together.

regnerisch
regnerisch. Das Wetter ist regnerisch.
Das Wetter ist regnerisch.

Write reg-ner-isch. The beginning is regn, not regen. Finish with isch, including sch. In these sentences the describing word comes after ist or sind; use regnerisch unchanged. The other sentence words are supplied: you only fill in the describing word.
Der Tag ist regnerisch.
Picture rain over your village. Regen means rain. Compare Regen and regnerisch: rain becomes the describing word rainy.
Write reg-ner-isch. The beginning is regn, not regen. Finish with isch, including sch.

kühl
kühl. Es ist kühl.
Es ist kühl.

Write k-ü-h-l. Keep both the two dots over ü and the silent h after it. In these sentences the describing word comes after ist or sind; use kühl unchanged. The other sentence words are supplied: you only fill in the describing word.
Der Morgen ist kühl.
Picture a cool autumn morning when you need a light jacket. Kühl is cool in temperature, not English cool meaning awesome.
Write k-ü-h-l. Keep both the two dots over ü and the silent h after it.
Picture the scene, hide the word, and write kühl from memory. Check it letter by letter.
wasserdicht
wasserdicht. Die Jacke ist wasserdicht.
Die Jacke ist wasserdicht.

Build wasser + dicht with no space. Wasser has double s; dicht ends cht. Lowercase w. In these sentences the describing word comes after ist or sind; use wasserdicht unchanged. The other sentence words are supplied: you only fill in the describing word.
Die Gummistiefel sind wasserdicht.
Picture water rolling off your rain boots. Wasser is water; dicht can mean sealed. Together, wasserdicht means waterproof.
Build wasser + dicht with no space. Wasser has double s; dicht ends cht. Lowercase w.
Picture the scene, hide the word, and write wasserdicht from memory. Check it letter by letter.
dicht
dicht. Der Nebel ist dicht.
Der Nebel ist dicht.

Write d-i-c-h-t. Keep cht together; there is no second i or final e. In these sentences the describing word comes after ist or sind; use dicht unchanged. The other sentence words are supplied: you only fill in the describing word.
Der Wald ist dicht.
Picture fog packed so closely that you cannot see the next tree. Dicht means dense here. It can also mean sealed, as in wasserdicht; the sentence tells you which meaning fits.
Write d-i-c-h-t. Keep cht together; there is no second i or final e.

der Spaziergang
der Spaziergang. Der Spaziergang ist kurz.
Der Spaziergang ist kurz.

der Spaziergang means walk / stroll. die Spaziergänge means walks / strolls. Keep Spazier unchanged; Gang → Gänge: a → ä, then add -e. Write Spa-zier-gang. The long ee sound in zier is written ie. In Wir machen einen Spaziergang, masculine ein changes to einen because the walk receives the action. Learn the whole noun with its article. All German nouns start with a capital letter.
Wir machen einen Spaziergang.
die Spaziergänge
Singular: der Spaziergang. Plural: die Spaziergänge. Keep Spazier unchanged; Gang → Gänge: a → ä, then add -e.
For one, say der Spaziergang; for more than one, say die Spaziergänge.
Picture a relaxed stroll around your village, rather than a long hike. Spaziergang is the walk; Wanderung is the hike. Gang can mean a walk or going.
Write Spa-zier-gang. The long ee sound in zier is written ie. In Wir machen einen Spaziergang, masculine ein changes to einen because the walk receives the action.
Picture the scene, cover the German, and write der Spaziergang. Check every letter and the article.
die Ernte
die Ernte. Die Ernte ist gut.
Die Ernte ist gut.

die Ernte means harvest. die Ernten means harvests. Add -n to Ernte. Write Ern-te: keep r, n, and t in that order. Start with capital E and end with e. Learn the whole noun with its article. All German nouns start with a capital letter.
Die Ernte ist im Herbst.
die Ernten
Singular: die Ernte. Plural: die Ernten. Add -n to Ernte.
For one, say die Ernte; for more than one, say die Ernten.
Picture gathering pumpkins and crops from the field. That harvest is die Ernte. The same Ernte starts Erntedankfest.
Write Ern-te: keep r, n, and t in that order. Start with capital E and end with e.
Picture the scene, cover the German, and write die Ernte. Check every letter and the article.
der Drachen
der Drachen. Der Drachen fliegt.
Der Drachen fliegt.

der Drachen means kite. die Drachen means kites. The noun spelling stays Drachen; change der → die for the plural. For a kite, write Dra-chen with ch and a final n. Both one kite and several kites keep that n. Learn the whole noun with its article. All German nouns start with a capital letter.
Der Drachen ist bunt.
die Drachen
Singular: der Drachen. Plural: die Drachen. The noun spelling stays Drachen; change der → die for the plural.
For one, say der Drachen; for more than one, say die Drachen.
Picture a colorful kite on a string in the wind. Keep its tail: the final n in Drachen. A mythical dragon is der Drache, without that final n in its singular name.
For a kite, write Dra-chen with ch and a final n. Both one kite and several kites keep that n.
Picture the scene, cover the German, and write der Drachen. Check every letter and the article.
die Gummistiefel
die Gummistiefel. Die Gummistiefel sind gelb.
Die Gummistiefel sind gelb.

der Gummistiefel means one rain boot. die Gummistiefel means rain boots / rubber boots. The noun spelling stays the same. One: der Gummistiefel. More than one: die Gummistiefel. Gummi has double m. Stiefel has ie for its long ee sound. Join them: Gummistiefel. With several boots use sind, not singular ist. Learn the whole noun with its article. All German nouns start with a capital letter.
Singular: der Gummistiefel. Plural: die Gummistiefel. The noun spelling stays the same. One: der Gummistiefel. More than one: die Gummistiefel.
For one, say der Gummistiefel; for more than one, say die Gummistiefel.
Picture a pair of rubber boots splashing in a puddle. Gummi means rubber; Stiefel means boot. Your lesson gives the plural: die Gummistiefel. One boot is der Gummistiefel.
Gummi has double m. Stiefel has ie for its long ee sound. Join them: Gummistiefel. With several boots use sind, not singular ist.
Picture the scene, cover the German, and write die Gummistiefel. Check every letter and the article.
